scams.name: Shoe Bet Hustle
scams.description: A couple was strolling through the French Quarter on their first night in New Orleans when a man with a shoeshine kit stepped into their path and said with a big grin, 'I bet you five dollars I can tell you where you got your shoes.' The husband, certain there was no way a stranger could know where he bought his sneakers back in Ohio, took the bet. The man immediately replied, 'You got your shoes on your feet, and your feet are on Bourbon Street.' Before anyone could laugh it off, the hustler was already kneeling down, spraying something on the shoes and wiping them with a rag — no actual polish, just water — then demanding $20 for the 'shine' on top of the $5 bet. When they tried to walk away, a second man appeared and blocked them, insisting they pay up. Multiple r/AskNOLA threads and Tripadvisor forums describe this as the single most iconic New Orleans street scam, operating continuously for decades around Jackson Square, Bourbon Street, and the entire French Quarter. Variations include betting they can guess the exact street, the city, or even 'what state your shoes are in.'
scams.avoidance: Never accept a bet from a stranger on the street — the answer is always a wordplay trick Keep walking and say 'no thanks' without slowing down or making eye contact If someone compliments your shoes or asks about them, that is the opening move — disengage immediately Do not let anyone touch your shoes or kneel near your feet under any circumstances If pressured, walk toward a crowd or an open business — scammers avoid making scenes near establishments
scams.location: Bourbon Street, Jackson Square, throughout the French Quarter

scams.name: Freestyle Rap Welcome
scams.description: A group of friends had just arrived from Texas and were walking down Decatur Street when a charismatic young man approached them with a huge smile and said, 'Welcome to New Orleans! Where y'all from?' They told him Dallas, and within seconds he launched into a surprisingly impressive freestyle rap incorporating their names, their hometown, and details they had casually mentioned. The whole group was laughing and clapping along — until the rap ended and the performer demanded $20 from each person, insisting they had agreed to pay by participating. When one friend said she never agreed to anything, the rapper got aggressive, calling her cheap in front of other tourists and physically blocking the sidewalk. Threads on r/travel and Carpe Travel's scam guide describe this as one of the top five New Orleans scams. The performers are genuinely talented, which makes the hustle work — tourists feel entertained and then guilted into paying far more than a street tip. Some operate with lookouts who identify groups and relay personal details overheard from nearby conversations.
scams.avoidance: If someone asks where you are from and seems overly enthusiastic, recognize it as the setup for this scam Do not share your name, hometown, or any personal details with strangers who approach you on the street A firm 'no thank you' while continuing to walk is the most effective response If a performance starts, you are under zero obligation to pay — walk away immediately If you genuinely enjoyed it, tip a dollar or two and leave — do not let anyone dictate a price after the fact
scams.location: Decatur Street, Bourbon Street, French Quarter, Marigny

scams.name: Three-Card Monte
scams.description: A man had a few drinks on Bourbon Street and noticed a small crowd gathered around a cardboard box near Canal Street where a guy was shuffling three cards and daring people to find the queen of spades. He watched a woman bet $20 and win easily — then another man bet $50 and won too. It looked simple. He put down $100, certain he was tracking the right card, but when it flipped over it was the wrong one. He tried again with his last $60 and lost that too. What he did not realize was that every 'winner' in the crowd was a shill — a planted accomplice whose job was to make the game look beatable. The dealer uses sleight of hand to ensure marks never find the right card. r/AskNOLA and multiple Tripadvisor threads explicitly warn about three-card monte setups near Canal Street and along the edges of the French Quarter, often operating on folding tables or cardboard boxes that can be collapsed in seconds if police approach. The game is illegal in Louisiana and is designed so that you mathematically cannot win.
scams.avoidance: Never gamble with street dealers — three-card monte is a rigged con, not a game of skill The 'winners' you see are always planted accomplices working with the dealer If a crowd has gathered around a card game on the street, walk the other direction Report street gambling operations to NOPD non-emergency line at 504-821-2222 Remember that any street game where money changes hands in New Orleans is illegal and almost certainly a scam
scams.location: Canal Street, edges of the French Quarter, Jackson Square area

scams.name: Bourbon Street Shot Girls
scams.description: It was past midnight on Bourbon Street when an attractive young woman approached a group of college friends with a tray of colorful shots in test tubes, shouting 'Shots! Shots! Who wants a shot?' She thrust one into a guy's hand before he could say anything and he instinctively drank it. She then demanded $20 for the single shot — a watered-down, barely alcoholic concoction that would cost $3 in any actual bar. When he balked at the price, she called over a large man who said the price was non-negotiable. In some versions documented on Tripadvisor's Bourbon Street review threads, the shot girls work in coordination with bar doormen who will threaten to call police on tourists for 'theft' if they refuse to pay. The drinks are heavily diluted and sometimes barely contain any alcohol at all. A review titled 'Stay away from the shots-in-a-test-tube girls' on Tripadvisor warns specifically about this practice, noting that some establishments actively participate in the hustle by letting shot girls operate just outside their doors.
scams.avoidance: Never accept a drink handed to you on the street — especially if you did not ask for it and the price was not stated Always ask the price before accepting any food or drink from a vendor on Bourbon Street If a shot is placed in your hand, put it down immediately and walk away Stick to buying drinks inside established bars where prices are posted or on a menu Never drink anything from someone you do not know on the street — it is also a basic safety issue
scams.location: Bourbon Street, French Quarter nightlife strip

scams.name: Bead and Bracelet Force
scams.description: A solo traveler was admiring the architecture near Jackson Square when a smiling woman approached and placed a string of colorful Mardi Gras beads around her neck, saying 'Welcome to New Orleans, baby!' Before she could react, a man appeared and tied a braided bracelet onto her wrist. They told her the beads and bracelet were a 'gift from the city' — then immediately demanded $20, claiming it was a donation for their church. When she said she did not want them and tried to remove the bracelet, the man grabbed her wrist and insisted she could not give them back because they were 'blessed.' A second woman moved closer, creating a tight circle. The traveler, feeling intimidated and alone, paid $15 just to get away. Posts on r/solotravel and multiple travel blogs describe this scam as common around Jackson Square and the Riverwalk, with scammers specifically targeting solo travelers and women. The beads cost pennies — they are the same mass-produced plastic beads thrown for free during Mardi Gras parades.
scams.avoidance: Do not allow anyone to place anything on your body — step back immediately if someone reaches toward you Keep your hands in your pockets or crossed when walking through heavy tourist areas If someone drapes beads on you, remove them and place them on the ground — you owe nothing for an unsolicited item Travel with a companion when possible, especially around Jackson Square and the Riverwalk You can buy authentic Mardi Gras beads for under $1 at any shop outside the French Quarter
scams.location: Jackson Square, Riverwalk, Bourbon Street, French Quarter entrances

scams.name: French Quarter Pickpocketing
scams.description: A couple was enjoying live music on Frenchmen Street around 1 AM when a group of young men started an argument right next to them. While everyone's attention was on the commotion, someone bumped into the husband from behind and apologized profusely. It was not until they got back to their hotel that he realized his phone and wallet were gone from his back pocket. According to a 2024 NOLA.com article, French Quarter thefts and pickpocketing surged 70 percent, with NOPD issuing a specific public warning about organized pickpocket teams operating on Bourbon Street and between Bourbon and Frenchmen Street. The professionals work in groups of three or four — one creates a distraction such as a staged fight, a spilled drink, or an overly friendly greeting, while the others move in to lift phones, wallets, and purses. Intoxicated tourists late at night are the primary targets. Police reports document suspects stealing phones and immediately sending themselves money through payment apps before the victim even notices.
scams.avoidance: Keep your phone in a front pocket or a zippered crossbody bag — never in a back pocket or dangling from your hand Use a money clip with only the cash you need for the night and leave cards locked in your hotel safe Be especially vigilant after midnight when alcohol has impaired your awareness and thieves are most active If a stranger bumps into you or creates a commotion nearby, immediately check your belongings — that is the classic distraction technique Avoid walking alone on side streets between Bourbon and Frenchmen after dark — stick to well-lit main thoroughfares
scams.location: Bourbon Street, Frenchmen Street, Canal Street, throughout the French Quarter after dark

scams.name: Name-Spelling Bet
scams.description: A family of four was walking near the Cafe Du Monde when a charming man stopped them and said, 'I bet you ten dollars I can spell your last name.' The father, whose surname was an unusual Eastern European name, laughed and said there was no way. He told the man his first name was Kevin. The hustler grinned and said, 'Your last name? Easy — L-A-S-T-N-A-M-E. That is twelve letters and it spells last name.' The man held out his hand for the $10. When Kevin protested that was not what he meant, the hustler insisted a bet was a bet and followed the family for half a block, loudly calling them cheapskates. This is documented on Carpe Travel's guide and multiple Tripadvisor New Orleans forum threads as a companion scam to the shoe bet — sometimes the same hustler will try both in sequence. A variation asks, 'I bet I can tell you how many letters are in your last name' — the answer is always 'twelve,' because the words 'your last name' contain twelve letters. It is a low-stakes annoyance but can turn aggressive if you engage and then refuse to pay.
scams.avoidance: Never agree to any bet with a stranger — the answer is always a trick based on wordplay Do not give your name to anyone who approaches you uninvited on the street If someone asks you a riddle or a question that sounds like easy money, walk away — you will always lose Pair this awareness with the shoe bet — these hustlers often work in the same areas and try multiple cons Keep a polite but firm 'not interested' ready and do not break stride
scams.location: French Quarter, near Cafe Du Monde, Jackson Square, Bourbon Street
